hooks: Everyone's excited about autonomous supply chain agents. Gartner is also predicting that over 40% of those projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.
The agent didn't fail. The data foundation under it did.
Supply chain software with agentic AI is going from under $2 billion in spend to $53 billion in five years. Over 40% of the projects built on it won't survive that long.
drafts.caption:
Everyone's excited about autonomous supply chain agents. Gartner is also predicting that over 40% of those projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.

Read the reason list. Model capability isn't on it.

The causes Gartner names:
→ No governance structure - nobody owns the call when the agent's decision is wrong
→ No clean data foundation - the agent inherits the same broken master data your planners have fought for years
→ No success metric attached - the "pilot" never had a number that decided if it graduated

Meanwhile the market is real. Supply chain management software with agentic AI capability is projected to grow from under $2 billion in spend in 2025 to $53 billion by 2030, per Gartner. Organizations that get the foundation right are already reporting double-digit efficiency gains and decision latency cut from days to seconds.

Same technology, opposite outcome. The difference isn't the vendor demo - it's whether someone owns the exception queue on a Tuesday morning.

Before you approve the next agent pilot: who signs off when it's wrong, and what number decides if it's still live in twelve months?

hooks: 77% of pharma supply chain leaders now rank AI-driven demand sensing for new launches as a top priority. Most are still feeding it the same three inputs as 2019.
A launch forecast built only on sales history is already six months late on day one.
Pharma leaders aren't asking if AI can forecast demand anymore. They're asking if it can forecast a launch nobody has sold before.
drafts.caption:
77% of pharma supply chain leaders now rank AI-driven demand sensing for new launches as a top priority, according to the LogiPharma 2025 AI Report, a survey of 100 senior leaders across Europe and North America.

But a launch has no sales history. That's the actual problem a demand-sensing model has to solve.

The teams getting it right aren't just swapping the forecasting engine. They're changing the inputs:
→ Prescription and market-access data instead of only shipment history
→ A rolling SKU-channel-region forecast that updates weekly, not a static plan set once a quarter
→ Predictive risk alerts on the supply side - 53% of leaders are now using AI/ML here, up from roughly 30% two years earlier

The same report names the real blockers, and none of them is the model: internal resistance (70%), regulatory uncertainty, and a shortage of people who can read the model's output and act on it before the batch record closes.

If your last launch forecast was wrong, was it the algorithm - or the input nobody updated after month one?

hooks: Deloitte expects agentic AI adoption on the factory floor to roughly quadruple this year, from 6% to 24%. Only about one in five manufacturers say they're ready to scale it.
The sensor predicted the bearing failure twelve days out. The work order still sat in an inbox for nine of them.
Predicting the failure was the easy part. Nobody automated what happens after the alert.
drafts.caption:
Deloitte expects agentic AI adoption on the factory floor to roughly quadruple this year, from 6% to 24%. Only about one in five manufacturers say they're actually ready to scale it.

That gap isn't about the sensor. Most plants can already predict a bearing failure, a motor overheating, a line about to go down.

What's missing is what happens in the days between the alert and the fix:
→ Who owns the work order once the model flags it
→ Which spare part gets reserved automatically instead of requested by email
→ What triggers a line-speed change while the fix gets scheduled

Predictive maintenance without an owned, automated response is a dashboard nobody acts on until the line stops anyway. It's the same failure mode Gartner points to across agentic AI projects broadly: the model works, the decision loop around it doesn't.

The plants closing that gap aren't buying a better model. They're assigning a name to the alert.

When your last predictive-maintenance alert fired, how many hours passed before anyone with authority touched it?

hooks: The FDA's first AI warning letter didn't blame the AI. It blamed the missing signature.
An AI agent wrote the batch specs. Nobody wrote a control to check them. That's the whole warning letter.
Everyone's asking whether AI can draft GMP documents. In April, the FDA answered a different question: who's accountable when it does.
drafts.caption:
The FDA's first AI warning letter didn't blame the AI. It blamed the missing signature.

In April, the FDA sent Purolea Cosmetics Lab a warning letter with a section the agency had never written before: "Inappropriate Use of Artificial Intelligence." The firm had used an AI agent to draft specifications, procedures, and master production and control records.

The citation wasn't that AI touched GMP documents. It was 21 CFR 211.22(c) - the firm didn't review the AI's output for accuracy before it went into use. Separately, the agent missed a process-validation requirement under 211.100, and nobody caught it before the inspection did.

Read that twice. The AI didn't fail its job. Someone skipped theirs.

If you're piloting AI to draft batch records, specs, or CAPAs inside your quality system, the lesson isn't to stop. It's to name, in writing, who reviews the output before it becomes a controlled record - and to be able to show that the review happened, not just that a box got checked.

An AI draft is a draft. Your quality unit still signs it.

Who in your quality system is named as reviewer of record for anything AI drafts, and can you point to their sign-off on the last one?

hooks: 58% of maintenance teams are already using AI. 79% of them saw unplanned downtime stay flat or get worse.
Two numbers, same plant, moving in opposite directions - AI adoption up, downtime not down.
75% of maintenance teams say their AI tool paid for itself in under six months. Their downtime log tells a different story.
drafts.caption:
58% of maintenance teams are already using AI. 79% of them saw unplanned downtime stay flat or get worse.

That's from MaintainX's 2026 State of Industrial Maintenance report, a survey of 2,234 maintenance and operations leaders across the US and Canada. 75% of teams using AI say they saw measurable ROI within six months. Meanwhile 45% report the same downtime as a year ago, 34% report more, and 39% say downtime got more expensive - up from 31% in 2025.

Two numbers, same plant, moving in opposite directions. The report's own explanation isn't the model. It's the people around it:
→ Labor shortages leave predictive alerts unassigned
→ Retiring veterans take undocumented troubleshooting knowledge with them
→ Weak handoffs mean a flagged failure sits in a queue nobody owns

A sensor that predicts a bearing failure twelve days out doesn't help if the work order takes nine of them to get picked up. The ROI shows up on the software invoice before it shows up on the line.

If your AI maintenance tool is already paying for itself on paper, what does your actual downtime log say for the same six months?

hooks: AI is now embedded in fulfillment, inventory, and customer experience at most omnichannel retailers. MIT's newest survey says most of them funded it in the wrong order.
647 supply chain leaders were surveyed. The ones seeing returns didn't start with the flashiest AI use case.
Everyone wants the AI that personalizes the offer. MIT's data says fix the inventory number first.
drafts.caption:
AI is now embedded in fulfillment, inventory, and customer experience at most omnichannel retailers. MIT's newest survey says most of them funded it in the wrong order.

MIT's Center for Transportation and Logistics surveyed 647 supply chain professionals for its 2026 State of Omnichannel Supply Chain Report. AI already touches demand forecasting (63%) and customer experience (64%), with personalization leading the list - 69% for marketing, 66% for recommendations, 66% for segmentation.

But personalization raised the bar on the layer underneath it: 65% of respondents now say they need real-time product availability, and 63% report higher inventory-accuracy requirements than before. MIT's own recommendation to leaders is blunt - fund the areas with proven ROI first, starting with inventory accuracy and fulfillment, before the AI use cases built on top of them.

A recommendation engine trained on a wrong on-hand number doesn't get smarter. It gets confidently wrong, faster, at scale.

Before the next AI budget line gets approved: does it fix the inventory number, or does it sit on top of one you already don't trust?
